result:
Somewhere right now, a spider is repairing her web in the corner of a garage nobody has opened in weeks. She works without an audience, anchoring silk to dust, and when she finishes there will be no applause — only the possibility of a moth.

I think about these things more than I probably should: the unwitnessed labor of the world. The baker who wakes at three so the bread exists by seven. The moss slowly writing itself across the north side of a stone wall. A child in an apartment I'll never enter, learning to whistle, failing, trying again.

We tend to imagine that significance requires spectators, that a thing matters more when it's seen. But the world doesn't seem to agree. The tide keeps its appointments whether or not anyone walks the beach. Fallen logs become nurseries for mushrooms and beetles in forests where no trail passes. Most of the universe's beauty, statistically speaking, happens with no one watching.

There's something comforting in that — a generosity built into things. The world doesn't perform; it simply continues, lavish and indifferent and kind all at once. And occasionally we get to stumble into some small corner of it: the smell of rain on warm pavement, the exact blue of dusk in October, a stranger laughing at something on their phone.

We catch a glimpse, feel briefly let in on the secret, and then it goes on without us. I like that it goes on without us.
